## Abstract {.unnumbered}

We build a neural-operator layer whose temporal kernel, for every spatial Fourier mode k, is a sum of poles and
residues that are polynomials in k. A trained layer can therefore be read as a dispersion relation λ(k). The time
axis is a first-order-hold exponential-integrator recursion: exact for piecewise-linear inputs, causal, and
independent of the window length. As a representation it is about 100× more accurate than the Fourier time axis
of Laplace neural operators on smooth non-periodic inputs (Appendix A).

**Linear systems.** In 1D diffusion, advection–diffusion–reaction, an undamped Euler–Bernoulli beam, and 2D
diffusion and anisotropic ADR, the layer recovers the dispersion relation at the data's oracle floor in every
seed. It does so either through a two-stage identification or through a joint fit from random starts. Three
details decide success:

- scaling the polynomials in $k/k_{\mathrm{ref}}$, with a second-order optimizer;
- excluding modes that the window or the sampling cannot resolve;
- a leaky cap on Re μ, because a hard cap traps starts.

**Nonlinear systems.** A deep version (lifting, channel-mixing pole layers, pointwise nonlinearities) is tested on
forced viscous Burgers, on PDEBench 1D Burgers and on forced KdV–Burgers (dispersive, complex poles).

- It trains only with a separate, larger learning rate for its poles.
- At a matched budget it beats a band-covering Tucker FNO by 2× with 50 training samples, by 9 % with 400, and
  by 7× in time extrapolation.
- A small-amplitude linear probe recovers ν to 1–3 %. The FNO baselines are right inside the forced band but
  produce arbitrary poles outside it.
- **The form is what pays.** The same operator with a free pole per mode index (the per-mode generators of
  state-space and spectral-generator operators) matches the in-band accuracy and the time extrapolation, but its
  error on unseen forcing modes is 181× its test error (95 % interval 106–255, 5 seeds), against 1.3× (0.9–1.6)
  with poles in k. An S4D-type SSM operator, ALNO, LFNO and the original LNO, run at the same budget, have
  unseen-mode errors 3.6–114× their test errors and are 1.6–14× less accurate than the WPO (5 seeds each).
- With complex poles (forced KdV–Burgers) the same holds: the WPO recovers the dispersion coefficient within 4 %
  in every seed, and its unseen-mode error is 2.1× its test error against 20–364× for the per-index form, the TFNO
  and an SSM operator.
- On PDEBench 1D Burgers the Tucker FNO is 1.8× more accurate at an equal real-parameter budget. The FNO block
  closes half of that gap; the rest is consistent with whole-window temporal mixing, which a causal time axis
  gives up. A hybrid that keeps the WPO's linearization does not close it.

**Pole laws.** A polynomial pole law extrapolates outside the forced band when its form is right; an MLP law wins
in band when it is not, and fitting both is a check.

A companion paper applies the layer to Cahn–Hilliard phase separation.

## Introduction

Laplace-type neural operators [@cao2024lno; @ha2026lfno] represent the transient response with learned poles,
which invites a physical reading of those poles. The companion audit (project C) found that this reading fails by
default: poles do not move under published protocols, and fits are equally good with wrong poles. Project A asks
the constructive question. If the pole structure is made explicit in the wavenumber, can a model identify the
system's dispersion relation, and does that structure pay off in accuracy, data efficiency or extrapolation
against Fourier neural operators [@li2021fno]?

**Related work.** Several recent operators learn a stable linear generator per spatial Fourier mode:
structured state-space models keep diagonal poles per channel [@gu2022s4; @gu2022s4d] and serve as neural
operators for dynamical systems [@hu2025ssmno]; SGNO [@li2026sgno] learns a multiplier per Fourier index with an
exponential-integrator update; LGN-KM [@jamil2026lgn] ties a latent Koopman generator's damping to |k|^p and reads
dispersion branches from it, for unforced flows. "Poles per Fourier mode" is therefore not what is new here. The
claim of this paper is narrower: the poles are smooth functions μₙ(k) of the *physical* wavenumber in an
input-driven operator with an exact time axis, which is what makes them identifiable, continuable outside the
excited band and transferable across domain sizes. @sec-form tests that claim against free per-index poles in the
same architecture, and against an S4D-type SSM operator, LNO, ALNO and LFNO at the same budget.


**Parameter budgets.** All budgets are counted in real degrees of freedom. The FNO-type baselines up to a35 were
matched by `numel`, which counts a complex weight once; their real budgets were 1.5–1.9× the WPO's. Reruns at
equal real budgets change no conclusion: on forced Burgers the smaller TFNO is slightly better (a36). The tables
below give the original runs; the reruns are in the experiment records.

**Scope.** This paper covers the layer, its identification on linear systems, deep operators on Burgers and
KdV–Burgers and the choice of pole law. Process dynamics (delays, reactors, closed loops) and the Cahn–Hilliard application (the spinodal band, 2D
forced and coarsening dynamics, transfer across domain sizes) are separate papers.

Every experiment below was pre-registered: predictions were committed before the runs, and every failed
prediction is reported.

## The wavenumber pole layer {#sec-layer}

For a linear PDE u_t = L u + f with periodic space, every Fourier mode obeys $d\hat u_k/dt=\lambda(k)\,\hat u_k+\hat f_k$. The layer
models the temporal kernel of mode k as

$$K(k,s)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{\beta_n(k)}{s-\mu_n(k)},\qquad
\mu_n(k)=\sum_j a_{nj}\,(k/k_{\mathrm{ref}})^{2j}+i\sum_j c_{nj}\,(k/k_{\mathrm{ref}})^{p_j},$$

with $\beta_n(k)$ a polynomial in k². The parameters are continuous in k, so the layer runs on any spatial grid.

- **Time axis.** The exact first-order-hold recursion $x_{j+1}=E\,x_j+b_0u_j+b_1u_{j+1}$, evaluated as a causal
  FFT convolution plus a first-sample correction. It is exact for inputs that are linear between samples, causal,
  and needs only Δt, so the same layer runs on a longer window or a finer Δt. On non-periodic inputs the
  Fourier time axis of LNO costs 4e-4 to 2e-3 as a representation (Appendix A).
- **Options.**
  - `modes`: truncation to the forced band.
  - `re_max`: a smooth cap on Re μ. With `re_leak`, it keeps a slope above the cap (@sec-trap).
  - `stable`: Re μ = −softplus.
  - Any powers of k in Im μ: the beam's frequency c k² is even.
- **2D.** Re μ is a polynomial in |k|², and Im μ = c · k plus optional $|k|^p$. A real field needs
  μ(−k) = conj μ(k). The rfft2 layout holds negative $k_x$ only on the row $k_y = 0$, so the even imaginary terms get a
  half-plane sign there; tests caught the error before this was added.
- **Deep operator.** lift → [$K_l + W_l$, GELU] × L → projection. $K_l$ mixes channels, with N poles shared by all
  channel pairs and a residue matrix per pole. Summing the poles into one frequency-domain kernel per channel pair
  makes training 2.5× faster, with identical outputs.

### Domain and window consistency {#sec-consistency}

Write $\Phi_{L}$ for a deep WPO on a periodic domain of length L, at grid spacing h and band $|k|\le K_c$. When L
changes, `set_domain` rescales the mode count, so the physical band stays the same. Write $P_s$ for the map that
reads an L-periodic field as an sL-periodic one ($s\in\mathbb N$, same spacing). On the grid this is tiling s
times.

**Proposition (consistency).**

(a) *Domain.* $\Phi_{sL}\circ P_s=P_s\circ\Phi_L$ exactly.

(b) *Window.* For $T'>T$ at the same Δt, the output of $\Phi$ on $[0,T']$ restricted to $[0,T]$ equals its
output on $[0,T]$ from the restricted input.

The solution map $S$ of any autonomous, translation-invariant evolution equation with unique solutions has both
properties, linear or not. Hence on inputs of the form $P_s f$, the relative error on the large domain equals the
relative error on the training domain. Tiling scales both norms by $\sqrt s$.

*Proof.*

- *Domain.* $P_s f$ has Fourier support on $(2\pi/L)\mathbb Z\subset(2\pi/(sL))\mathbb Z$, with the same coefficients
  under the FFT normalization. Each pole layer multiplies mode k by a temporal kernel that depends only on k, and
  the band selects the same physical k on both grids. Lifting, channel mixes, activations and projection act
  pointwise, and the sL grid is s copies of the L grid, so every block commutes with $P_s$. Induction over the
  blocks gives (a).
- *Window.* Every block is causal. The FOH recursion uses only Δt and past samples, and the pointwise parts act
  sample by sample. This gives (b).
- Uniqueness and translation invariance give $S_{sL}P_s=P_sS_L$; autonomy and causality of the evolution give (b)
  for $S$. ∎

**Index-parametrized operators.**

- *Domain (a).* A spectral layer with a weight $R_m$ per mode index m has property (a) only if $R_{sm}=R_m$ on
  the band. On the sL grid, $P_sf$ occupies the indices sm, so the layer applies $R_{sm}$ where $R_m$ was learned.
  Its band shrinks to $|m|\le m_c/s$ in units of the old index.
  - Example: a layer that has learned exact diffusion, $R_m=e^{-\nu(2\pi m/L)^2\Delta t}$, still applies $R_m$ at
    index m. On the sL grid that index is the physical wavenumber $2\pi m/(sL)$, whose true factor is
    $e^{-\nu(2\pi m/(sL))^2\Delta t}$. Every resolved mode therefore decays $s^2$ times too fast.
  - This is the mechanism behind a Tucker FNO's failure on a box twice as large in the companion paper.
- *Window (b).* An FNO's temporal Fourier modes over the padded window break (b). This is the whole-window mixing
  that carries part of its accuracy on PDEBench (a40).

**Beyond tiled inputs.**

- A general sL-periodic input also excites the wavenumbers between the training ones, and there the layer is
  evaluated off its training grid. For a single linear layer whose pole law has the form of the truth (polynomials
  in k² of degree d), agreement at d + 1 distinct training |k| implies agreement at every k in the band. Otherwise
  the error at a new k is the interpolation error of the law, which the in-band probe bounds only at the training
  wavenumbers.
- For deep nonlinear operators no such bound is offered. The 2D transfer of the companion paper (1.02–1.03× the
  training-domain error; a34) is empirical.
- Property (a) and the causality behind (b) are tested in `tests/test_wavenumber.py` (tiled fields under
  `set_domain`; causality of the layer and of the deep operator).

## Linear systems {#sec-linear}

**Data.** Periodic x, 64 points, T = 5, n_t = 201. Each sample is forced at a few random modes with step, ramp,
PRBS or smooth time profiles. The truth is computed on a 32× finer time grid, so data and layer share no hold. The
oracle floor (the true λ in the layer) is 0.8–1.2 % and is set by jumps that fall between samples.

![Stage-1 per-mode poles against the truth (data seed 0). Filled: modes kept by the two cuts; hollow: modes cut
(too fast for Δt, or too slow for the window). Right: the beam's two poles per k; the cut modes k = 1–3 are where
the first beam recipe failed.](fig_linear.png){#fig-linear width=100%}

### A joint fit with Adam fails; the problem is optimization, not representation

The first validation fitted the polynomial jointly with Adam (a1).

- On diffusion, 3 of 5 seeds recover D to 0.02 % at the oracle floor. The other seeds, and every ADR seed, end in
  wrong basins with spurious k³, k⁴ terms.
- With k up to 16, one Adam step on a k⁴ coefficient moves Re μ by up to 6.5e4 × lr.

### A two-stage recipe recovers every system (a2–a6)

1. **Stage 1:** one pole per excited k (grid search, then Nelder–Mead; the residue by least squares).
2. **Stage 2:** weighted least squares for the polynomial.
3. **Fine-tune:** L-BFGS on the layer, with coefficients in $k/k_{\mathrm{ref}}$ units.

Two cuts, computed from the stage-1 estimates alone, decide which modes enter stage 2 (@fig-linear):

- a **resolution cut**, $|\hat\mu|\,\Delta t \le 0.25$ (fast modes are biased by the sampling);
- an **observability cut**, $\max(|\mathrm{Re}\,\hat\mu|, |\mathrm{Im}\,\hat\mu|)\,T \ge 2$. Slower modes fit as well with wrong poles; on the beam
  they wrecked 2 of 5 seeds before the cut was added.

With both cuts, every run in every system reaches the oracle floor:

| system (5 seeds each) | test / oracle | recovered constants |
|---|---|---|
| 1D diffusion, ADR | 0.98–1.10 | D, v, k_r within 0.05 % |
| beam (N = 2, poles ±i c k²) | 1.00–1.02 | c within 0.35 %, Re/Im ≤ 2.3e-4 |
| 2D diffusion, anisotropic ADR | 1.000–1.002 | D, v = (0.4, −0.3) within 0.03 % |

: Linear validations with the two-stage recipe and both cuts. {#tbl-linear}

### Stage 1 is not needed; a hard cap traps starts {#sec-trap}

A joint fit from 8–16 random starts, with the same $k_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and L-BFGS and selection by validation error, also
reaches the oracle in all 25 data seeds (a7).

- The failing starts were the same indices in every data seed. They ended with Re μ at the cap for all k, where
  the soft minimum has no gradient.
- A leak of 0.05 above the cap fixes it (a8): every start succeeds for diffusion and ADR, and 9–15 of 16 for the
  beam.
- Stage 1 remains useful as a model-free diagnostic and as a deterministic start.

## Deep operators on nonlinear systems {#sec-deep}

**Forced viscous Burgers** (ν = 0.1, 64 points, T = 5). The forcing scale is log-uniform over [0.03, 1], so up to
91 % of a sample is not the linear response. Linearized at u = 0, λ(k) = −ν k².

**Probe.** Single-mode inputs at small amplitude; the odd part of the response; the stage-1 identification per
mode; both cuts.

### The poles need their own learning rate

At a shared Adam learning rate (1e-3), the poles stayed at their initialization (a9). Re μ was flat in k, some
poles had Re μ > 0, and errors over (5, 10] blew up to 3–8. The k² coefficient of −ν k² is −25.6 in k / k_ref
units, beyond reach in 4000 steps. A pole learning rate 30× larger cut the error 2.4–3.4× (a10), as (C) found for
LNO.

### Accuracy, extrapolation and data efficiency

The first FNO baseline (n_modes 12 × 12) kept only |k| ≤ 6 and 7 temporal frequencies: below the forced band. We
found this after the run and replaced it with band-covering baselines (a13). Both models then got the same
learning-rate sweep.

| model | params | test (N = 200) | error over (5, 10] | probe residual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO (stable) | 59.5 k | **0.024** | **0.04** | **0.003** |
| TFNO (Tucker, n_modes 32 × 64) | 110.6 k real (59.1 k numel) | 0.031 | 0.29 | 0.008–0.25 |
| TFNO, real budget (a36) | 54.6 k | 0.028 | 0.29 | – |
| FNO (full rank, 18×) | 1.08 M | 0.042 (overfits) | 0.29 | 0.36–0.49 |

: Forced Burgers, 3 seeds; time extrapolation from training on T = 5 to T = 10. {#tbl-burgers}

![Forced Burgers: test error against training-set size (mean and min–max over 3 seeds; nested training sets, same
test set).](fig_data_eff.png){#fig-data width=50%}

- **Data efficiency** (@fig-data, a14): the TFNO / WPO error ratio is 1.96 at N = 50, then 1.42, 1.28 and 1.09 at
  N = 400. The WPO's advantage is an inductive bias, and it shrinks as data grow.
- **Resolution** (a15): every model transfers to 32 and 128 points within 9 %. At Δt/2 the WPO's error drops by
  20 %, the FNOs' by 4–8 %.

### What the probe reads

![Per-mode probe poles on forced Burgers, seed 0. Inside the forced band (shaded) every model is right; above it
only the WPO continues −ν k². The FNO variants return arbitrary poles. Beyond the resolution cut (dashed) the
estimates are biased for every model, the solver included.](fig_probe.png){#fig-probe width=60%}

- **Burgers.** Every model's linearization is right to 1–2 % inside the forced band (@fig-probe). Outside it, only
  the WPO continues the dispersion relation (k = 9 within 1–4 %), and only its small-amplitude response is
  LTI-consistent (residual 0.003).
- **A bias that was not physics.** An earlier probe bias (ν̂ 11–14 % high, a10) was the polynomial summary
  absorbing over-damping at the weakly forced top of the band. It vanished with longer training (a11). A
  polynomial summary needs its residual reported.

### Is it the physical-wavenumber form? (a36) {#sec-form}

Same data, same architecture and training as the WPO, but each layer's poles are a free table over the 22
retained mode indices (residues stay polynomial): the per-mode generator of S4D- or SGNO-type operators. Two
extra tests: the probe's poles outside the forced band (k = 9–16), and a set forced only at k = 9–12, which no
training sample excites. Four operators of the related work are added at the same real budget (a45): an
S4D-type SSM operator (the authors' S4D layer along t, a spectral convolution along x), the original LNO (v2,
steady modes raised to cover the band), and ALNO and LFNO with separable poles in x and t.

| model | test | (5, 10] / test | probe outside the band (k = 9–16) | unseen modes / test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO, poles in k | **0.024** | **1.85** [1.76, 1.95] | **0.10** [0.06, 0.14] | **1.3** [0.9, 1.6] |
| WPO, poles per index | **0.023** | **1.75** [1.67, 1.83] | 0.98 [0.95, 1.01] | 181 [106, 255] |
| TFNO, real budget | 0.029 | 10.0 [9.2, 10.9] | 0.87 [0.78, 0.97] | 31 [19, 42] |
| S4D-type SSM | 0.039 | 2.6 [2.1, 3.1] | 1.00 [0.90, 1.10] | 29 [24, 35] |
| ALNO | 0.077 | 4.1 [3.6, 4.7] | > 10 (every seed) | 114 [−29, 258] |
| LFNO | 0.094 | 166 [−187, 519] | > 10 (every seed) | 9.2 [7.9, 10.6] |
| LNO v2 | 0.32 | 1.4 [0.9, 1.8] | 1.08 [0.96, 1.19] | 3.6 [2.0, 5.3] |

: Forced Burgers; 5 seeds each, mean [95 % t-interval] (a42, a45); probe column: mean relative pole error against −νk². {#tbl-form}

- Inside the forced band the form does not matter: same test error, same time extrapolation (the FOH recursion
  carries it), and every model's probe is right at k ≤ 8.
- Outside it only the polynomial poles continue. Per-index poles at modes the data never excite stay where they
  started, and an input there produces a response 4× the truth's size.
- Every per-mode or per-index generator (the WPO's own per-index form, S4D, ALNO, LFNO, LNO) has an out-of-band
  probe error of order 1 or worse and an unseen-mode error 3.6–181× its test error.
- The S4D-type operator is the strongest baseline, but at equal budget the WPO is 1.6× more accurate. The original
  LNO does not fit forced Burgers at this budget (14× the WPO's error); ALNO and LFNO reach 3–4×.
- a36: five of six predictions held; the LNO's predicted extrapolation ratio above 2.5 failed because its in-window
  error is already large. a45: three of six held; two failures overestimated the SSM (predicted within 1.6× of the
  WPO's test error: 1.63×; predicted below the WPO on PDEBench: above), the third underestimated the spread of
  ALNO's unseen-mode error (interval not separated).

### A public benchmark: PDEBench 1D Burgers (a37)

Initial field → trajectory (ν = 0.01, 256 × 41, PDEBench's split and nRMSE). The repository solver reproduces the
benchmark to 3e-4 through an exact rescaling, so the linearization is known: λ_m = −0.1257 m².

- The Tucker FNO (equal real budget) is 1.8× more accurate: nRMSE 0.0254 [0.0247, 0.0261] against 0.0450
  [0.0440, 0.0459] (5 seeds, 95 % intervals; a42). Both are unchanged at 4× the resolution. The other baselines
  (a45) are less accurate than the WPO: S4D-type 0.0513 [0.0485, 0.0541], ALNO 0.088, LFNO 0.27 (one seed of five
  did not train; 0.118 without it), and the original LNO does not train (0.88). None has ν' within 5 % in any seed.
- The probe separates the models less than on forced Burgers: both get the slowest modes (m ≤ 4); at m = 8–10 two
  WPO seeds are within 10 % and no FNO seed is. The WPO's ν is within 5 % in 1 of 5 seeds; the prediction of 5 % in
  every seed failed. Without forcing that isolates modes, the data constrain the small-amplitude response only
  partly.
- The pre-registered WPO runs ended in nan from an overflow in a masked branch of the time kernel for very fast
  poles; the reported runs repeat them unchanged after the fix (post hoc).

### A dispersive system: forced KdV–Burgers (a47) {#sec-kdv}

Burgers' linearization has real poles only. Forced KdV–Burgers, u_t + u u_x = ν u_xx − δ u_xxx + f (ν = 0.1,
δ = 0.01), linearizes to λ(k) = −νk² + iδk³: at k = 8 a forced mode turns by about a radian while it decays. The
protocol is the forced-Burgers one of @sec-form unchanged; the data are more nonlinear (median nonlinear part 8.5 %,
90th percentile 49 %). The WPO's default pole form (Re in k², Im in k and k³) contains λ; the solver's own probe
recovers ν to 0.5 % and δ to 0.85 %.

| model | test | (5, 10] / test | unseen modes / test | probe outside the band | δ̂ / δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO, poles in k | 0.0245 | **1.83** [1.73, 1.93] | **2.1** [1.1, 3.1] | **0.21** [0.04, 0.38] | 1.03 |
| WPO, poles per index | **0.0227** | **1.80** [1.68, 1.93] | 364 (168–946) | 0.99 [0.97, 1.01] | 1.01 |
| TFNO, real budget | 0.0338 | 8.8 [7.5, 10.2] | 20 [14, 25] | 0.87 [0.81, 0.93] | 0.84 |
| S4D-type SSM | 0.0404 | 2.9 [2.5, 3.2] | 38 [22, 54] | ≥ 0.99 | 0.80 |

: Forced KdV–Burgers; 5 seeds each, mean [95 % t-interval] (per-index unseen ratio: seed range, its interval reaches below zero); probe outside the band: mean of |μ̂ − λ| / |λ| over k = 9–16. {#tbl-kdv}

- The Burgers picture holds with complex poles. In band every model's probe is right (dispersion error over
  k = 2–8: 0.015–0.018; post hoc, since the pre-set kept-mode cut admits spurious slow fits at unexcited modes
  here). The WPO recovers δ within 4 % and ν within 1.2 % in every seed; the TFNO and the SSM recover δ within 10 % in
  3 and 2 of 5.
- On unseen forcing modes the WPO's worst seed (3.3×) is 4.6× below the best seed of any other model (15×).
- The continuation is weaker than on Burgers: the out-of-band pole error is 0.21 (0.10 on Burgers), from k ≥ 14,
  where the fitted k³ term overshoots Im λ.
- Predictions: four of six held. The out-of-band error was predicted ≤ 0.2 (0.208). The unseen-mode interval was
  predicted to separate from every other model's; it separates per seed but not by the pre-set 95 % interval for
  the per-index form, whose ratio spans 168–946.

### Is the gap the missing odd symbol? (a39)

Even residues and pointwise channel mixes leave no part of the WPO that applies the derivative symbol i k, which
Burgers' convection needs. Two minimal changes, both at the WPO's real budget, test this: residues with odd powers
of k, and a 5-tap convolution over x in place of the pointwise mix.

- Neither closes the gap on PDEBench: 0.047 and 0.054 against the WPO's 0.045 and the FNO's 0.026. Four of six
  predictions failed, including both that predicted a gain.
- Odd residues keep the form's benefits on forced Burgers: test 0.025, probe outside the band 0.12, and unseen
  modes at 2.0× the test error.
- Local mixing does not. Its stencil is a symbol in k Δx learned in the band, so the probe outside the band rises
  to 0.32, unseen modes to 7.5×, and the error at 4× the resolution to 1.29×.
- The gap is therefore not in the linear symbol. The remaining candidates are the nonlinear block and the time
  axis: the FNO's temporal Fourier modes mix the whole window.

### Where the gap comes from: block and time axis (a40)

The neuraloperator FNO differs from the WPO in two ways beyond its spectral weights. Its block adds a channel MLP
with a gated skip, which gives it two nonlinearities per layer. Its time axis mixes the whole window, with t as an
input. Three variants at the WPO's real budget separate the two:

| model | PDEBench nRMSE | dispersion error |
|---|---|---|
| WPO | 0.045 | 0.24 |
| WPO with the FNO block | 0.036 | **0.17** |
| FNO without channel MLP | 0.030 | 0.63 |
| FNO over x per time sample (no temporal mixing) | 0.037 | 0.64 |
| FNO | **0.026** | 0.67 |

: PDEBench 1D Burgers, 3 seeds (means), equal real budgets. {#tbl-gap}

- The FNO block closes half of the gap at no cost: resolution invariance is kept, and the probe improves.
- Without temporal mixing the FNO loses more than half of its edge. The rest of the gap therefore lies in the
  time axis: a whole-window method can use the trajectory non-causally, and the WPO's recursion does not.
- That accuracy is what the causal axis pays for time extrapolation and for exact forcing semantics.
- Two of four predictions held. The MLP's share on the FNO side and the time axis's share were both misjudged.
- On forced Burgers the FNO block gains nothing (0.024 against 0.024; a41). In one seed of three it loses the
  probe outside the band (3× off at k = 16), so we do not adopt it as the default block.

### A hybrid that keeps the linearization (a49)

If the missing accuracy were nonlinear, a hybrid could add it without touching the form. H = W + E adds to a WPO W
the even part of a Tucker FNO T, E(f) = (T(f) + T(−f))/2 − T(0). E has no linear term, so H's linearization at rest
is exactly W's, while E supplies the even-order terms with whole-window temporal mixing. The plain sum W + T is the
ablation. Both are at the WPO's real budget, 5 seeds.

| model | PDEBench nRMSE | dispersion error | forced Burgers test | probe outside the band |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| WPO | 0.045 | 0.25 | **0.024** | **0.10** |
| W + even part of T | 0.047 | **0.16** | 0.036 | 0.40 |
| W + T | 0.028 | 0.68 | 0.029 | 0.51 (median) |
| FNO | **0.025** | 0.69 | 0.029 | 0.87 |

: The hybrid (a49), 5 seeds (means). {#tbl-hybrid}

- The even hybrid does not close the gap (0.047 against 0.045), although its probe improves, as with the FNO block
  in a40.
- The plain sum reaches the FNO's accuracy and, with it, the FNO's probe: its FNO branch takes over the linear
  response, and the probe ν′ falls to 0.043 against the truth 0.126.
- So the remaining gap is carried by the odd, whole-window part of the FNO, the part the pole form with a causal
  time axis excludes. It is a cost of the form (this reading is post hoc).
- On forced Burgers the even branch costs accuracy and the out-of-band probe (0.40), though the probe reads W
  alone: at half the budget and fitted jointly with E, W's poles are less constrained outside the band.
- Two of six predictions held; both predicted gains of the even hybrid failed. Three of four selections are at
  the upper edge of the learning-rate grid.


## Polynomial or MLP pole functions (RQ4) {#sec-rq4}

The plan offers an MLP μ(k) as the flexible alternative. To compare the two, we train only on data forced at k ≤ 8
and test at k = 9–16 (a19; diffusion, ADR, beam; 5 seeds; same joint fit).

- In band, both reach the oracle (MLP ≤ 1.05×).
- Out of band, the polynomial stays at 1.00–1.08× the oracle with a dispersion error ≤ 0.5 %. The MLP is at 4.6–44×
  with 13–55 %.

When the form is right, the polynomial wins on both accuracy and interpretability.

With a dispersion relation that is not polynomial, fractional diffusion λ = −0.15|k|^1.5 (a22), the order reverses:

- Trained on k ≤ 16, the MLP is at 1.02–1.04× the oracle and the polynomial at 5.4–8.5×.
- Out of band, neither extrapolates. The wrong polynomial is catastrophic there (3500×, driven by its k⁴ term); the
  MLP degrades to 12–18×.

This gives a practical check: fit both. If the polynomial matches the MLP in band, its form is supported and its
extrapolation can be trusted. If not, use the MLP and do not extrapolate.

## Discussion

- **What is identifiable.**
  - In linear problems, the full dispersion relation, from data alone, given scaled parameters and modes that the
    window and the sampling resolve.
  - In deep nonlinear models, the linearization at rest, through a probe, inside the forced band. That is true of
    FNO-type models as well.
  - What the pole structure adds: a dispersion relation that continues outside the forced band, and an
    LTI-consistent linear response. Free poles per mode index do not give this (@sec-form): the gain comes from
    the physical-wavenumber form, not from having poles. This holds for complex, dispersive poles (@sec-kdv),
    where the continuation is shorter: a cubic imaginary part fitted in band overshoots at k ≥ 14.
- **Where the accuracy gain comes from.** Data efficiency (2× at 50 samples) and time extrapolation (7×). The
  in-window error at 400 samples is close to parity (9 %).
- **Where the structure pays, and where it does not.** It pays in identification of dispersion relations,
  in continuation outside the forced band, and, when the law has the right form, in extrapolation of the pole law
  (@sec-rq4). Consistency across domain sizes is exact for tiled inputs (@sec-consistency); the companion paper
  tests it on 2D coarsening.

  It does not pay in pointwise accuracy on PDEBench Burgers, where the Tucker FNO is 1.8× better at an equal real
  budget. Odd residue powers or local mixing do not close this gap (a39); the FNO's block closes half of it on
  PDEBench but not on forced Burgers, and the rest is consistent with whole-window temporal mixing (a40, a41).
  A hybrid that adds only even-order FNO terms, and so keeps the WPO's linearization, does not close it; a plain
  sum does, at the cost of the FNO's linear response (a49).
- **Training details decide the outcome**, as in the companion audit (project C):
  - scaling the polynomials;
  - a pole learning rate in deep models;
  - a leaky rather than hard cap on Re μ;
  - checking that a baseline's modes cover the band. We got this wrong once.

## Limitations {.unnumbered}

- Two 1D nonlinear systems (viscous Burgers, forced and PDEBench's unforced set; forced KdV–Burgers), each with a
  known linearization at rest. The Cahn–Hilliard results, including the 2D experiments, are in the companion
  paper.
- Cost: in float64 the WPO takes 4.4–5× the TFNO's (float32) time per training step and 1.6–1.7× its memory
  (a43). The factor is precision: in float32 (poles, FOH coefficients and pole parameters kept in float64) its
  step is 1.0–1.05× the TFNO's on forced Burgers and 1.3× on PDEBench, with less memory than the TFNO, and the
  form claim and PDEBench accuracy are unchanged within the 5-seed intervals (a44; the PDEBench float32 runs are a
  post hoc rerun after a GPU FFT defect was fixed). Per-index poles cost the same as poles in k.
- One parameter budget (59 k); FNO-type baselines from neuraloperator with a learning-rate sweep but no
  architecture search. Up to a35 the baselines were matched by `numel` (1.5–1.9× the WPO's real parameters);
  the key comparison was rerun at equal real budgets (a36) with the same conclusion.
- One public benchmark (PDEBench 1D Burgers), unforced. The SSM baseline uses the authors' S4D layer inside our
  (x, t) operator, not a published S4D operator; ALNO and LFNO are our implementations in (x, t); SGNO-type
  operators are represented by the per-index form only. Learning rates were swept over 1e-4 to 1e-1 where the
  first grid's edge was selected; no selection changed (a46, a48).
- The probe is a small-amplitude linearization at u = 0.
- Appendix A compares time axes on linear single layers only.
- The oracle floor of the data (steps and PRBS between samples) limits every test error to about 1 %.

## Appendix A: the time axis for non-periodic inputs {.unnumbered}

The Fourier time axis of Laplace neural operators computes the response to the trigonometric interpolant of the
input samples, which assumes that the input repeats at the window ends. Steps, ramps and PRBS do not.

**Representation alone.** Without any training, we computed the response of known pole–residue systems (two to six
poles, including lightly damped complex pairs and fast real poles) to 100 inputs per family with each time-axis
representation. The inputs are defined on a 32× finer grid and seen only at the samples.

| input family | Fourier (LNO) | Fourier, pad 2× | FOH | Chebyshev 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| step | 1.7–2.8e-3 | 1.6–2.7e-3 | 1.6–2.7e-3 | 7.3e-3–1.1e-2 |
| ramp | 0.7–1.8e-3 | 1.8–2.9e-4 | **1.2–2.8e-6** | 1.0–1.6e-4 |
| PRBS | 0.9–1.0e-2 | 0.9–1.0e-2 | 0.9–1.0e-2 | 2.9–4.5e-2 |
| smooth, mismatched ends | 4.1–6.7e-4 | 3.0–4.9e-4 | 5.9–7.5e-6 | **1.7–2.2e-8** |
| periodic (control) | 2.9–4.5e-6 | 2.9–4.4e-4 | 1.8–4.0e-5 | **0.5–1.2e-7** |

: Median relative L2 error of the representation alone (three systems; ranges over systems). {#tbl-app-time}

- The Fourier path's error on non-periodic inputs is 10–100× its error on the periodic control. It is spread over
  the whole window rather than concentrated at the ends, and it falls only as $n^{-1}$.
- On steps and PRBS every path is limited by the sampling: a jump between samples cannot be located.
- A global Chebyshev fit is the best representation on smooth inputs. It is numerically unusable at high degree
  (errors up to 1e7 at degree 256) and poor at discontinuities.

**Trained layers.** The difference matters only once training reaches the representation floor. Under the
published LNO training protocol the training error (3e-3 to 4e-2) is 10–1000× the representation error of either
path. Trained to convergence on the same data, with fine-grid truth, single Fourier and FOH layers reach the same
test error, the sampling floor (3.7e-3 against 3.4e-3). A large FOH advantage seen on data generated with a
first-order hold was a model-class match, not a property of the time axis.

**Choice.** The FOH recursion is the default time axis, with piecewise Chebyshev as an option for smooth inputs.
It is never worse than the Fourier path except on periodic inputs, and it is causal, O(n), and independent of the
window length. The time extrapolation and the Δt transfer of the main text rest on that independence; the accuracy
gain on non-periodic inputs is a property of the representation, not of trained models.
